title: The Heart Plans, the LORD Directs
summary: The chapter opens with the densest group of sayings about the LORD in the whole collection: people make plans, weigh their own motives, and cast lots, but the LORD weighs hearts, establishes steps, and decides outcomes. A matching group of sayings follows on the king, whose justice and favor mirror God's rule. The rest of the chapter gathers famous sayings on pride before a fall, pleasant words, gray hair as a crown, and the patient person who is better than a warrior.
story: Chapter 15 ended on the fear of the LORD and humility (15:33). Chapter 16 opens by showing why humility fits: whatever a person plans, the LORD has the last word. Many scholars see this chapter as the beginning of the second half of the Solomonic collection, where the sharp but-contrasts of chapters 10 to 15 give way to a wider mix of forms. It also sits near the middle of the whole book, and its theme, human freedom exercised under God's rule, is one the rest of the book keeps returning to (19:21; 20:24; 21:1, 30-31).
historical:
Verses 10 to 15 speak of the king in a way that fits Israel's monarchy and ancient Near Eastern royal ideals generally. The king was the highest judge, and his word could mean life or death (verses 14-15). Verse 10 uses a striking word: the divine verdict on a king's lips is, in Hebrew, qesem, a word normally used for divination, which the law forbade (Deuteronomy 18:10). Here it seems to describe the king's decision as carrying the weight of an oracle, and the saying immediately adds the condition: his mouth must not betray justice. Israel's own history, including David's failures and Solomon's later forced labor, shows how often that ideal was missed.

Verse 11 returns to the merchant's scales and the stone weights carried in a bag. The claim that all the weights in the bag are the LORD's concern goes further than earlier sayings: honest measure does not merely please God, it belongs to his order of the world. Kings in the ancient Near East set standards for weights (2 Samuel 14:26 mentions weighing by the royal standard), which may explain why this saying sits among the sayings about kings.
cultural:
Verse 33 describes casting lots, a common way in the ancient world of reaching a decision that no one could manipulate. Marked stones or sticks were shaken in the fold of a garment (the lap) and thrown or drawn out. Israel used lots to divide the land among the tribes (Joshua 18:10), to identify a guilty party (Joshua 7:14-18; Jonah 1:7), and, in the priest's Urim and Thummim, to seek the LORD's answer (Exodus 28:30). The early church used a lot to choose Matthias (Acts 1:26). The saying does not endorse gambling; it says that even outcomes that look random fall under God's rule.

Verse 31 reflects the respect ancient Israel gave to old age. Gray hair was a crown of glory, the visible sign of a long life, which the book regards as a fruit of righteousness. The law commanded Israel to rise before the gray-headed and honor the aged (Leviticus 19:32).
literary: The chapter is carefully arranged. Verses 1 to 9 each name the LORD except verse 8, and they are bracketed by two sayings with the same shape (verses 1 and 9): the human heart plans, but the LORD gives the answer or directs the steps. Verses 10 to 15 each speak of the king, except verse 11, which the arranger seems to have placed there because weights were a royal responsibility. Verses 16 to 19 prize wisdom and humility over wealth and pride, including two better-than sayings. Verses 20 to 24 concern pleasant and persuasive speech. Verses 27 to 30 sketch four types of troublemaker: the worthless man, the perverse man, the violent man, and the one who winks. The chapter closes as it opened, with the LORD's rule over human decisions (verse 33). Verse 25 repeats 14:12 word for word.

outline.t: Human plans and the LORD's direction
The just king and the king's favor
Wisdom above gold; pride before destruction
The way of death, hunger, and four troublemakers
Gray hair, self-control, and the lot in the lap

doctrines.note: The chapter's opening and closing sayings (verses 1, 9, and 33) teach that God's rule runs through ordinary human decisions without canceling them. People truly plan and choose; the LORD truly determines outcomes. Proverbs holds both without explaining how they fit.

Verse 6 says that by loving devotion and faithfulness iniquity is atoned for. Proverbs does not set this against sacrifice but reminds the reader that God's forgiveness and a life of covenant loyalty belong together, and that turning from evil goes with it.
The LORD has made everything for its purpose (verse 4), and every decision of the lot is from him (verse 33). His sovereignty reaches kings (verses 10-15) and the smallest outcome alike.

words.note: Kipper, to atone, make atonement. It is the central verb of Israel's sacrificial system and the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16). Its basic sense is disputed: to cover, to wipe clean, or to pay a ransom. In verse 6 it appears outside the temple, linked with chesed and faithfulness, a reminder that atonement is God's gracious answer to sin, received in a life turned toward him.

Goral, lot. The word first means the stone or marker used in casting lots and then, by extension, the portion assigned by lot, as when the tribes received their land. Verse 33 uses it in the first sense, and its point is that even this apparently random act has its decision from the LORD.

Kun, to establish or make firm. The verb appears three times: commit your works and your plans will be established (verse 3), the LORD establishes a man's steps (verse 9), and a throne is established through righteousness (verse 12). What lasts is what God makes firm.

Ga'on, pride. The word can describe majesty in a good sense, including God's own majesty (Exodus 15:7), but when a human claims it for himself it becomes arrogance. Verse 18, pride goes before destruction, is one of the best known lines in the book.

christ: The chapter's picture of a just king whose lips speak God's verdict and whose throne is established by righteousness (verses 10-12) describes the ideal that Israel's kings kept failing to reach. The prophets looked for a son of David who would rule with righteousness and justice (Isaiah 9:7; 11:1-5), and the New Testament presents Jesus as that king. The saying that the heart plans but the LORD directs the steps (verse 9) finds its deepest example in the cross: Peter told the crowd at Pentecost that Jesus was handed over by God's set plan and foreknowledge, and yet by lawless human hands (Acts 2:23). Human choices and God's purpose met there, as this chapter says they always do. Verse 32's praise of the one slow to anger fits the one who, when insulted, did not retaliate (1 Peter 2:23). These are connections of theme and pattern rather than predictions.

hard.q: Verse 4 says the LORD made even the wicked for the day of disaster. Does God create people in order to destroy them?
hard.a:
The verse sits inside a larger Christian debate about God's sovereignty and human responsibility, and readers answer it differently. Some, especially in the Reformed tradition, read it as teaching that God's purposes include even the end of the wicked, and they link it with Paul's discussion in Romans 9. On this reading God is not the author of evil, but nothing, including judgment on the wicked, falls outside his plan. Others point out that the Hebrew phrase rendered for His purpose can mean for its answer or for its counterpart, and read the verse as saying that God has made everything to have its fitting outcome: the wicked are matched to the day of disaster, as crime is matched to consequence. On this reading the verse is about moral order, not about God creating people for destruction.

Both readings agree on what the verse does not say. It does not make God responsible for anyone's wickedness, since verse 5 immediately holds the proud accountable, and it does not deny that the wicked can turn, which the whole book urges them to do. How God's rule and human choice fit together is a question on which faithful Christians have long differed.

questions: Verse 9 says the heart plans but the LORD determines the steps. How do you hold your plans when you believe this?
Verse 18 is one of the best known sayings in the Bible. Where have you seen pride go before a fall, in your own life or in public life?
Verse 32 says the one who rules his temper is greater than one who captures a city. Why might self-control be harder than conquest?
